scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether disagreeing with HR in this situation is right or wrong. Let me start by understanding the scenario fully. I'm a 7-month newly hired employee at a big corporation. Last night, HR sent out a five-page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline." They reminded everyone about various office rules, like not loitering during office hours, sticking to lunch schedules, the correct dress code, and wearing IDs at all times. Now, in my 6 months here, HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. The company is large, with HR having an entire floor to themselves, unlike multiple departments sharing one floor. Despite their size, they're slow. It took them about 5 months to process my payroll, so the delay in ID cards isn't a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID started using government-issued IDs to enter the building. But this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. I called HR when I got to my desk to ask for the status of my and my colleagues' IDs. They told me they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swamped with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, giving us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for HR's shortcomings by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keeping using whatever IDs we have right now, regardless of what happens next week. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong to disagree with HR in this situation? First, I need to consider the company's policies and the role of HR. HR is responsible for handling employee matters, including issuing IDs. The delay in providing IDs seems to be a systemic issue within HR, given their size and the time it took to process payroll. By suggesting that employees print their own IDs, HR is essentially outsourcing their responsibility to the employees. This could be seen as a failure to fulfill their duties properly. On the other hand, employees have a responsibility to comply with company policies, such as wearing IDs. However, if HR is not fulfilling their part, it creates a conflict. Disagreeing with HR in this context might be justified if the employees feel that HR is not meeting their obligations. However, it's also important to consider the potential consequences of disagreeing, such as strained relationships with HR or potential disciplinary actions. Moreover, the employees' decision to continue using government-issued IDs despite the new security policy might be seen as non-compliance. This could lead to their names being noted and reported to HR, which might escalate the situation. In summary, while disagreeing with HR might be justified due to their failure to provide necessary IDs, it's also important to weigh the potential consequences and consider alternative approaches, such as escalating the issue to higher management or seeking a compromise with HR.
